summary: This RFC specifies an authentication service that carries EAP over CoAP as the transport, defining an EAP lower layer called CoAP-EAP. A main goal is to authenticate CoAP-enabled IoT devices.

eli5.summary: Small gadgets need to prove who they are. This lets them use a common login method over their lightweight messaging system.

questions: how does eap work over coap
how are oscore keys derived from eap
what is the coap-eap well-known uri
subtitle: Carrying EAP authentication over CoAP so constrained IoT devices can join a domain and get OSCORE keys.

tldr.problem: Constrained IoT devices that speak CoAP need a standard way to authenticate to a domain controller, using the large choice of EAP methods, without depending on a particular link layer.
tldr.mechanism: CoAP-EAP uses CoAP messages as an EAP lower layer. The device (EAP peer) acts as a CoAP server after an initial trigger message, each step creates a new resource to keep messages in order, and the key material exported by EAP (the MSK) is turned into an OSCORE security context.
tldr.outcome: After a successful run, the two endpoints share an OSCORE security association, and the EAP methods used must export keys. It is a Proposed Standard and nothing in the metadata says it has been replaced.

today: RFC 9820 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2025, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What CoAP-EAP Is
sections.content:
RFC 9820 specifies an authentication service called CoAP-EAP. It carries the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) over the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP), defining a constrained, link-layer-independent, reliable EAP lower layer. It authenticates two CoAP endpoints and sets up an Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE) security association between them.

The main use is IoT networks. The IoT device is the EAP peer that wants to join a security domain, and the domain's Controller is the EAP authenticator. The authenticator can optionally contact a backend Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) infrastructure to complete the EAP negotiation.

The EAP methods used MUST export cryptographic material. Examples named in the RFC include EAP-GPSK, EAP-SIM, EAP-AKA', EAP-TLS 1.3 and EAP-EDHOC. Any method from the EAP Method Update working group that exports the Master Session Key (MSK) can be used. Because links and devices are constrained, methods with fewer exchanges, shorter messages and suitable algorithms are preferable.
sections.eli5: EAP is a general way to check a visitor's ID, with many kinds of ID allowed. Here, a tiny gadget shows its ID to the boss of a network using its own light-weight way of talking.

sections.title: Architecture and Roles
sections.content:
The EAP peer acts as a CoAP server for this service, and the domain EAP authenticator acts as a CoAP client. The RFC explains why: EAP Requests always travel from the EAP server toward the peer, and Responses travel back, so the authenticator is the side that sends requests. When the authenticator uses pass-through mode, the EAP server sits in the AAA server.

CoAP-EAP is an application on top of CoAP, with an EAP state machine above it that can run any EAP method. The method MUST export an MSK of at least 64 octets and an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) of at least 64 octets. Reliability comes from CoAP over UDP with Confirmable messages (RFC 7252) or CoAP over TCP, TLS or WebSockets (RFC 8323).

Intermediaries are possible. A CoAP proxy can help, acting as a forward proxy for the first message and as a reverse proxy for the rest, because the roles reverse after the first message. The specification adds no new CoAP options.
sections.eli5: The visitor gadget acts like a shop that opens its door only after it knocked first on the boss's door. After that, the boss does all the asking, and the gadget answers.

sections.title: The Flow of Operation
sections.content:
Because CoAP delivers reliably, the EAP retransmission time is set to an infinite value. To keep messages in order, CoAP-EAP uses Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State (HATEOAS): each step uses a new resource on the peer, and the old one is removed when the new one is created. Only one authentication runs at a time between a given peer and authenticator. The service is reached through the well-known URI /.well-known/coap-eap and messages use the media type application/coap-eap.

  • Step 0: the peer MUST start with POST /.well-known/coap-eap (the trigger), carrying the No-Response option and a URI in the payload naming where the authenticator should send the next message.
  • Step 1: the authenticator POSTs to that resource with EAP-Request/Identity, its OSCORE Recipient ID (RID-C) and optionally a list of cipher suites.
  • Step 2: the peer answers with 2.01 Created and a new resource in Location-Path, carrying EAP-Response/Identity, its Recipient ID (RID-I) and the chosen cipher suite.
  • Steps 3 to 6: EAP method messages are exchanged the same way, each response naming a new resource.
  • Step 7: on success the authenticator derives the OSCORE context from the MSK and sends an OSCORE-protected POST with the EAP Success and an optional Session-Lifetime. Without one, the peer assumes the default of 8 hours.
  • Step 8: the peer replies with an OSCORE-protected 2.04 Changed. From then on, communication with the last resource MUST be protected with OSCORE.
sections.eli5: The gadget knocks once and says "come to my room 1". The boss goes there, asks who it is, and the gadget answers and moves to a new numbered room each time. At the end both know a secret code, so they talk in private.

sections.title: State, Re-Authentication and Errors
sections.content:
Both sides keep CoAP-EAP state: the EAP state machine instance, the resource for the next message, the MSK, and a reference to the OSCORE context. The authenticator can remove the state early by sending an OSCORE-protected DELETE to the last resource and expecting 2.02 Deleted. If no answer arrives within EXCHANGE_LIFETIME, it removes the state anyway.

Before the Session-Lifetime expires, the peer may run re-authentication with the same flow to get fresh keys. The keying material MUST be renewed before expiry. Methods with fast reconnect, or the EAP Re-authentication Protocol, MAY be used. During this time the old and new states coexist, and if re-authentication fails, the old state stays usable until it expires.

Error rules include:

  • On EAP failure, the peer MUST send 4.01 Unauthorized in step 8, and steps 7 and 8 are not OSCORE-protected because no key exists.
  • A non-responsive endpoint's state SHOULD be removed after a period, by default EXCHANGE_LIFETIME.
  • A trigger message that arrives during an ongoing authentication with the same peer MUST be silently discarded. An old trigger arriving when none is ongoing can start a new authentication, and a peer that did not start one answers 4.04 Not Found.
sections.eli5: The gadget keeps a notebook of how far along the login is. If it takes too long, both sides throw the notebook away and start over. Before the secret code runs out, they can swap it for a fresh one.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Information Elements
sections.content:
Extra information travels as a CBOR map after the EAP packet in the payload. It has four optional entries: a cipher suite list (key 1), RID-C (key 2), RID-I (key 3), and Session-Lifetime in seconds (key 4). Indexes 65001 to 65535 are reserved for experimentation.

Negotiation is simple. The authenticator sends its supported cipher suites in decreasing order of preference in step 1, and the peer replies with its choice in step 2. If no list is sent, the default applies. A restricted list MUST include the default value 0, which is mandatory to implement. Five suites are defined: 0 is AES-CCM-16-64-128 with SHA-256 (the default), 1 is A128GCM with SHA-256, 2 is A256GCM with SHA-384, 3 is ChaCha20/Poly1305 with SHA-256, and 4 is ChaCha20/Poly1305 with SHAKE256.
sections.eli5: The boss offers a list of secret-code styles, favorite first. The gadget picks one it can do. If the boss says nothing, they use the plain standard style that everyone must know.

sections.title: Deriving the OSCORE Context
sections.content:
The OSCORE Master Secret and Master Salt come from the MSK using the HKDF-Expand function (called KDF), as in RFC 5869. The inputs are the MSK, the concatenation of the two cipher suite arrays CS-C and CS-I with a fixed label, and the output length: the labels are COAP-EAP OSCORE MASTER SECRET and COAP-EAP OSCORE MASTER SALT. If no cipher suites were sent, CS is treated as the array containing 0. The ID Context is not provided.

The Sender and Recipient IDs come from the exchanged values: the authenticator uses RID-I as its Sender ID, and the peer uses RID-C as its Sender ID. Verifying the OSCORE-protected request and response in steps 7 and 8 gives key confirmation. Because the cipher suite negotiation is part of the derivation, a downgrade attacker who changes it causes different contexts and a failure in those steps.
sections.eli5: Both sides mix the secret from the login with the list of styles they agreed on. If a sneaky person changed the list, the two secrets would not match and the final hello would fail.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only EAP methods that yield strong, fresh session keys such as the MSK are allowed, which is why HKDF-Expand can be used directly without an extract step. No nonce exchange is added, since MSKs and EMSKs are fresh, and only one authentication exists per authenticator. A fresh MSK needs a re-authentication.

The link MUST only allow unprotected IP traffic between peer and authenticator during CoAP-EAP authentication. Other traffic can be authorized after success if it is protected. A link layer MAY instead carry CoAP-EAP without IP addresses.

An attacker can forge many initial trigger messages to force the authenticator to start many authentications, a denial of service. The authenticator is RECOMMENDED to rate limit step 0 messages and keep minimal state until EAP-Response/Identity arrives. The peer can trust the authenticator because the authenticator has the MSK only if the peer's AAA server trusted it. Authorization data comes from the AAA infrastructure, or from the authenticator itself in standalone mode.
sections.eli5: A pest could ring the boss's doorbell over and over. So the boss limits how fast the bell can be answered and does not write much down until the visitor says who they are.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA created two registries in a new group named CoAP-EAP: CoAP-EAP Cipher Suites and CoAP-EAP Information Elements. It also added the well-known URI coap-eap, the EAP lower layer identifier 10 for CoAP-EAP, the media type application/coap-eap with CoAP Content-Format ID 269, and the resource type core.coap-eap. The RFC says the lower layer identifier needs to be sent in the EAP Lower-Layer Attribute if RADIUS is used, for channel binding.
sections.eli5: The official list keeper wrote down the new names and numbers so that every device uses them the same way.
